Scall
SKAWL
noun
From Middle English scalle, a scaly or scabby eruption, of Scandinavian origin (compare Old Norse skalli, a bald head). The Hebrew is netheq, a scab or tearing-off of the hair. In Leviticus it names the dry scall, a leprosy of the head or beard.

Biblical Definition

The scall is a scabby, scaly eruption of the scalp or beard, a species of leprosy that the priest was to examine and judge under the law of Leviticus 13. When it appears deeper than the skin... and there be in it a yellow thin hair; then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head or beard (Lev 13:30). If the priest could not at first discern its depth, he was to shut up the man seven days (Lev 13:31), and again on the seventh day to look whether the scall spread not (Lev 13:32), for the mark of true leprosy was its spreading. It stands in the closing summary as one of the plagues the law was given to govern: this is the law for all manner of plague of leprosy, and scall (Lev 14:54). Two things are noteworthy. First, the scall struck the head and beard—the crown of a man’s dignity, the place of his honor—and so pictures how sin lodges in the seat of pride and thought, defiling a man where he most prizes himself. Second, the diagnostic sign was spreading: a mark that stayed contained might be pronounced clean, but a mark that crept and widened was leprosy indeed. So sin is known: not merely by its first appearance but by its restless spreading, its refusal to stay small, its creeping into every hidden place of the life until the whole man is unclean. The priest’s patient inspection, the shutting-up, the second look, all teach that uncleanness is not a light matter to be waved away but a plague to be searched out; and the leper cleansed at last (Lev 14) points to the great High Priest who alone can pronounce the unclean clean.

Webster 1828 Definition

A scabby or scaly eruption of the scalp or beard; a leprosy of the head.

expand to see more

SCALL, n. [Middle Eng. scalle; of Scandinavian origin, akin to Old Norse skalli, a bald head.] A scab; a scaly or scabby eruption, especially of the scalp; a dry leprous affection of the head or beard.

In Scripture, the dry scall, a plague of leprosy upon the head or beard, to be examined and judged by the priest (Lev. xiii. 30-37).

Distinguished as clean or unclean by whether it spread beneath the skin and turned the hair yellow and thin.

Named in the summary of the law for all manner of plague of leprosy and scall (Lev. xiv. 54).

Figuratively, a creeping corruption that fastens on the head, the seat of a man’s dignity and pride.

Key Scripture

Lev 13:30 — "Then the priest shall see the plague: and, behold, if it be in sight deeper than the skin; and there be in it a yellow thin hair; then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head or beard."

Lev 13:31 — "And if the priest look on the plague of the scall, and, behold, it be not in sight deeper than the skin, and that there is no black hair in it; then the priest shall shut up him that hath the plague of the scall seven days:"

Lev 13:32 — "And in the seventh day the priest shall look on the plague: and, behold, if the scall spread not, and there be in it no yellow hair, and the scall be not in sight deeper than the skin;"

Lev 14:54 — "This is the law for all manner of plague of leprosy, and scall,"

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a law of uncleanness; it recovers how sin lodges in the seat of pride and is known by its spreading.

expand to see more

The present age has little patience for the priest’s slow work—the looking, the shutting-up, the second look on the seventh day—because it does not believe that uncleanness is a plague to be searched out at all. Sin, on the modern account, is a private matter that harms no one and spreads to no one; leave the mark alone and it will trouble no man. But the scall preaches otherwise. Its whole diagnosis turned on one question: did it spread? A contained mark might be pronounced clean; a creeping one was leprosy. So corruption is never content to stay small; it lodges in the head, the seat of thought and pride, and works outward until the whole man is defiled. To leave it unexamined is not mercy but folly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the patient, priestly searching-out of uncleanness—that sin fastens on the crown of a man’s dignity and betrays itself by spreading, and that it must be looked upon honestly, not waved away. The law that shut up the leper for inspection points to the great High Priest who searches the head and the heart, and who alone can pronounce the unclean clean.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A word for a scabby head-leprosy rooted in the Old Norse for baldness.

expand to see more

Middle English scalle—a scab or scaly eruption; of Scandinavian origin, akin to Old Norse skalli, a bald head.

Hebrew netheq—a scab, a scall, a tearing-off of the hair from the scalp.

The “dry scall”—a leprosy of the head or beard, judged by the priest in Leviticus 13.

Diagnosed by spreading: a mark that stayed contained was clean, a mark that crept was leprosy indeed.

Governed by the shutting-up and the seventh-day look, the patient priestly searching-out of uncleanness.

Usage

"The scall was judged not by its first look but by whether it spread beneath the skin."

"Sin, like the scall, fastens on the head—the seat of a man’s pride—and will not stay contained."

"The priest shut up the leper for a second look; God does not wave away uncleanness but searches it out."
